newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese builder collapses, third in two months.
newsitem.headline: Japanese builder collapses, third in two months.

text.p: Medium-sized Japanese contractor Daito Kogyo Co Ltd on Tuesday became the third listed Japanese construction firm in less than two months to collapse under debts left over from the late 1980s' asset price bubble.

Daito Kogyo, a Tokyo-based firm capitalised at 6.19 billion yen ($52.4 million), said it applied for court protection from creditors with debts totalling 159.2 billion yen ($1.34 billion), versus assets of 64.0 billion yen ($542.37 million).

Private research firm Teikoku Databank Ltd said Daito Kogyo, which expanded into condominium and office construction during Japan's so-called "bubble era" of inflated land and stock prices, failed to obtain financial support from creditor banks despite its difficulties.

Daito Kogyo's business deteriorated due to a slowdown in public works orders and private-sector contracts, as well as its lending and loan guarantees to troubled affiliated firms, Teikoku Databank said.
Analysts said that, while a growing list of Japanese builders was trying to devise plans to deal with heavy debts, medium-sized general contractors were likely to be squeezed further.

"The industry may have entered a long winter," said Toshihiko Okino, an analyst at Schroders Japan Ltd. "The hard times might continue for the next seven to eight years, like they did in the late 1970s to mid-1980s.
"There is no good news in the construction sector at all."
The seriousness of the sector's woes was highlighted in July, when two publicly listed general contractors, Tokai Kogyo Co Ltd and Tada Corp , collapsed under heavy debts.
Tokai Kogyo was the first to go, with debts of 511 billion yen ($4.33 billion).

A wave of business failures in the construction sector is anticipated as a result of the government's planned 10 percent cut in public-works spending over the three years from next April, analysts say.
Private-sector construction orders are also slowing due to Japan's fragile economic recovery, making it hard for general contractors to win profitable orders amid fierce competition.

In addition, analysts say banks are now taking a harder look at the financial health of each general contractor, and will soon be forced to let troubled builders go under as the Finance Ministry introduces stricter rules on assessing banks' bad assets. The new rules will go into effect with earnings reports for the year to March 31, 1998.
"The future of Japan's construction companies will depend on how their creditor banks act," said Yoshinobu Yamada, a banking analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.

Japanese banks have yet to set aside loan-loss reserves for potential problem loans to the construction sector, as many builders have managed to pay interest on their bank loans, even if the payments have fallen short of the required amounts.
Also, analysts say, despite their problems, most construction firms have continued to post yearly profits, a prerequisite for winning public works contracts from local governments. ($1=118 yen)
